newsitem.title: GERMANY: German employers slam Waigel's tax plan.
newsitem.headline: German employers slam Waigel's tax plan.

text.p: A leading German employers group has sided with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in criticising Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to increase taxes on overtime, night and holiday shifts in industry.

Dieter Hundt, president of the Federation of German Employers, told the daily Koelner Stadt Anzeiger that such a move would cause unit wage costs to rise at a time when industry required an easing in the cost of labour.

"This is a step in the wrong direction," said Hundt. "This form of taxation, of course, has the negative consequence that the costs of labour rise through the higher social security payments that are required."
Hundt also made clear that the government has raised the ire of Germany's powerful trade unions with this tax measure and as a result this year's wage rounds could prove difficult.
"I cannot rule out that this regulation will influence future wage rounds," he said.
The Bonn government had frustrated its own efforts to lower labour costs by implementing new social security payments such as the insurance for long-time nursing care.
But in the face of 4.6 million jobless, Germany needs to lower wage costs or risk falling further behind international competitors.
Kohl to meet SPD boss Lafontaine for tax talks

"The SPD is of the opinion that it is inexpensible for the economy and the labour market that income tax cuts are introduced for workers and families as soon as January 1, 1998," the party said in a statement. "That is why the SPD welcomes the appointment that was agreed today."
A German government spokesman, however, told the government's routine news conference that he knew nothing of such a meeting between Kohl and Lafontaine.

The spokesman also could not comment on a meeting earlier on Friday between Kohl and the leaders of his centre-right coalition and leaders from their respective parliamentary groups to discuss the planned tax reform.

The German government has proposed a net reduction in income taxes of 30 billion marks for 1999, but needs the support of the SPD to gain passage of parts of the plan in parliament. The SPD opposes some of the planned cuts and wants the whole programme brought forward by one year to 1998.
